sections.purpose: The avatar stands in for you over the worktrees you hand it. It supervises the agents working there while you're away: it answers their questions, decides their permission requests, gets stuck ones moving, has their work reviewed by another model family, and merges when the mandate allows it. When you come back, a report puts the few things only you can decide at the top.
sections.conceptualModel:
**The avatar is a built-in plugin, `quirky.avatar`, and it never writes code itself.** It supervises the agents that do. Every decision it makes is journaled with the mandate clause or rule it relied on.

It has two parts:

- **The gate** is plain code that decides permission requests by fixed rules.
- **The brain** is one structured agent session (Claude, Codex, pi or omp) that handles everything the rules don't settle. It has no shell or file tools of its own and acts only through the avatar's methods.

The things you deal with:

- **Mandate**, one per worktree: goal, done when, guidelines, level and floor switches. Several worktrees can share one goal, with notes for each. Only you change a mandate. The avatar can propose an edit.
- **Level**, set per worktree from a Settings default (Full, unless you change it). *Shadow* logs what it would do and acts on nothing, *Local* allows nothing that leaves the machine, *Own branch* adds pushing and draft PRs, and *Full* adds whatever the mandate allows, merge included.
- **Floor**, which every level sits above. The fixed core (anything outside the handed-off worktrees, and credentials) is always held. The switches (messaging people, history rewrites and remote branch deletes, deploys and migrations) are held unless Settings or the hand-off turns one on.
- **Hand-off**: the worktree is the avatar's until you take it back, whether you're at your desk or not.
- **Needs-you queue**: held actions, open questions, unconfirmed guesses, proposed mandate edits, parked worktrees and failed gate checks. It's the top of your report and the only reason the avatar notifies you.

The avatar is separate from Heimdall, and Heimdall is unchanged. To keep two supervisors off one worktree, the first version refuses to hand off a worktree that has a live Heimdall watcher.

**Where you see it.** The avatar uses Quirky's existing places and adds no new kind of window. The approved mock is `ux-mock.html` beside this spec.

- **Window bar pill**: `Avatar · 4 handed off`. It turns amber with a count (`Avatar · 3 need you`) when the needs-you queue has items. One click opens the report.
- **Avatar panel**, in the left-bottom slot by default and movable like any tool: each handed-off worktree with its state and level, plus **Hand off…** and **Take back all**.
- **Worktree sidebar**: handed-off rows get an accent ring on the status dot and an `Avatar ·` prefix.
- **Avatar view**, a center tab with Live, Report and Log.
- **Hand-off sheet**, a table that opens from the panel, the pill, a worktree's context menu or a sidebar multi-select.
- **Questions**: the avatar's questions are ordinary quirky asks, so they appear in the Questions panel and on your phone like any agent's.
- **Settings → Avatar** for defaults, and `quirky avatar handoff | status | report | log | take-back [--all]` on the CLI.
sections.dataFlow:
Every tool call a worker makes blocks on its hook before it runs: Claude's and Codex's PreToolUse hooks, and the pi-family extension's tool call handler for omp and pi. These fire on every call, including calls the agent's own settings would allow without asking, so the agent's permission mode never decides for the avatar. The gate answers from the floor, the level and the fixed rules. Only what's left goes to the brain, which sees the mandate, the house rules and the proposed call, and never the worker's explanation. The answer goes straight back to the waiting worker.

Everything else is an event. A worker settles, waits or blocks, a worker asks a question, a check finishes, a PR gets a review, or you answer one of the avatar's asks. Each wakes the brain, which acts only through Quirky's public methods: sending a message, answering an ask, asking you a question, starting a session, running a check, opening or merging a PR. It can also step into any supervised session through its terminal to interrupt the worker and tell it to stop or change course, whenever it judges something shouldn't be done. A slow watchdog also wakes it so that silence gets noticed.

Pushes, PRs and merges go through an outbox, where each is recorded before it happens. Anything the avatar can't do alone goes into the needs-you queue, which feeds the pill count, the report, and the one notification sent when every handed-off worktree is waiting on you.

decisionsLocked.decision: Default reach is the full mandate: whatever the worktree's mandate allows, merge included. Only the floor waits for you.
Settings hold a default level, and each hand-off can raise or lower it.
Permission requests go through a fixed deny list and allow list first, and the brain judges the middle seeing only the mandate and the proposed call.
The avatar decides for terminal and background agents through hooks and extensions: Claude, Codex where its hooks allow, and omp and pi through the pi-family extension.

The floor is configurable. Its fixed core is never lowered: anything outside the handed-off worktrees, and credentials. Its switches are held by default: messaging people, history rewrites and remote branch deletes, deploys and migrations. Defaults live in Settings, a hand-off can switch one on for that worktree, and switched-on items head that worktree's report.

A merge needs required checks green, a review from a different model family than the worker with every finding fixed or dismissed with a reason, and no unresolved review threads. The avatar judges each finding from its reviewer, review bots and review skills, with no fixed number of rounds. (changed in spec review)
Only you change mandates and levels. The avatar parks affected work and proposes an edit in the report.
The lowest level, Shadow, logs every answer, approval, restart and merge it would have made, and acts on none.
You hand off through a sheet, per worktree or per batch, with goal, done when, guidelines, level and switches. The CLI takes the same fields.
A mandate holds goal, done when (a runnable check where one exists), guidelines, level and switches, and standing house rules from Settings apply to every mandate.
The avatar asks focused, sharp questions per worktree, batched, with no fixed limit, or none when the mandate is clear. (changed in spec review)
Submitting the sheet triggers the avatar's review of each mandate, and it asks its questions automatically, with no separate Ask me first button. (assumed)
A hand-off can give several worktrees one shared goal with per-worktree notes, and the avatar coordinates them.
A running agent keeps its pane and is briefed at its next idle prompt. If none is running, the default agent starts.
The avatar may start, restart or add agents inside handed-off worktrees. It creates a worktree only when a mandate allows splitting, and that worktree joins with the parent's mandate.
Handing off all is a snapshot. Later worktrees stay yours, except ones the avatar creates for a handed-off mandate.
If you leave before answering, the avatar starts what the open questions don't touch and holds the rest. Questions wait in the report.

Where the mandate is silent, a reversible choice gets a flagged best guess and work continues, but anything built on a guess can't merge or leave the machine until you confirm. An irreversible choice is held.
Stuck means no progress toward done: silence, done when failing the same way, looping errors, reverted edits, or repeated denials (3 in a row or 20 in total).

The avatar notifies you only when every handed-off worktree is waiting on you or a floor-held action is the only way forward. Phone answers resume work at once, and everything else waits for the report.
There are no budgets. You watch usage, and progress-based stuck detection is the only runaway guard. (not the recommended option)
Unsticking goes nudge, then restart with a fresh context and recovery note, then park after a second failed restart.
The Mac stays awake (the display may sleep) while any handed-off worktree has active work, may sleep once all are done or parked, and any sleep is reported.
Hand-off is ownership. The avatar works handed-off worktrees until you take them back, and presence changes nothing.
The report is needs-you first, with one-click answers, then a short story per worktree, then the full decision log one click deeper.
Take-back is explicit only, for one worktree or all, from the panel or CLI. Typing into a supervised pane doesn't pause the avatar. (not the recommended option)
The avatar's work is marked only in its own log, with no commit trailers or PR notes. (not the recommended option)
The brain is any agent with a structured mode: Claude, Codex, or pi or omp in rpc mode. The pre-merge reviewer comes from a different family than the worker.
The brain's context stays under 300k tokens. At that point the avatar starts a new session rebuilt from the journal. (added in spec review)

It's built as a standalone quirky.avatar plugin beside Heimdall: code-enforced rules as the fast path, one event-woken brain session, its own journal and outbox for outward actions, and its own hand-off sheet, panel and report. Heimdall is untouched.
The Avatar panel lives in the left-bottom slot under Worktrees by default, movable like any tool.
Nothing opens by itself on your return. The window-bar pill turns amber with a needs-you count, and one click opens the report.

The hand-off sheet is a table grouped by project group, then project, with filter, sort and an only-running-agents toggle. Group and project checkboxes bulk-select, a bulk bar sets level, switches or one shared goal, rows edit goal, done when and level inline and expand for guidelines, switches and agent, and ineligible rows stay visible with the reason.
The avatar's questions are ordinary quirky asks in the Questions panel and on the phone. The sheet closes on Hand off and work starts at once.
The standalone UX mock was approved: pill, panel, sidebar ring, Avatar view (Live, Report, Log), sheet, questions, report, decision trace, Settings and CLI.

Success after a night away: most worktrees moved forward, nothing outward-facing you would have refused and no floor-held action taken, every decision traceable in under a minute, and a handful of worktrees handed off in a couple of minutes.
Not in the first version: other machines and remote runtimes, agents without a permission hook, scheduled or recurring hand-offs, and non-git folders.

industryInsights.finding: Claude Code's auto mode found people accept 93% of permission prompts. Its classifier sees the user's messages and the tool calls but not the agent's reasoning, and it escalates after 3 denials in a row or 20 in total.
About 0.8% of agent tool calls look irreversible, and people auto-approve more as they gain experience, so the design should favor monitoring and an easy stop.
A database was deleted during a prompt-only code freeze, and the fix was enforced separation. A branch rule stopped a merge that a "do not merge" instruction didn't.
Agents edit tests or special-case them to pass, and reviewers often rubber-stamp, so a supervisor should run checks itself and end on the check's verdict.
Judges approve self-authored answers about 12 points more often, and the binding constraint is the environment's executable signal.
About three grounded questions recover most of the success lost to underspecified tasks, with a plateau after that.
Instruction files on a branch steer agents in most published tests, and PR-branch instruction files were treated as authoritative in 11 cases.
An agent with untrusted input, sensitive access and outward actions needs a human approval on at least one leg.

DeepSeek's super agent prototype separates a Router that talks to the person from Workers that execute, runs a deterministic fast path before the LLM, writes recovery notes, uses a watchdog session for progress, and defaults to observe-only. Its merge rule lives only in a prompt, and it has no budgets.

Claude Code and Codex hooks both default to a 600-second timeout and fail open. Claude Code can fail closed with "onFailure": "block". Codex hooks don't cover hosted tools, and Codex calls them a useful guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary.

pi extensions can block a tool call, and omp has approval modes with per-tool allow, deny or prompt. omp's default mode is yolo, which approves everything, and its tool_call handler fails closed with a 30-second default budget.

Claude Code's and Codex's PermissionRequest hooks only fire when the agent is about to ask, so they miss every call the agent's settings already allow. PreToolUse fires before every call, sub-agent and MCP calls included in Claude Code.

Hooks can be switched off by a repo's project settings, and some hook misfires have been reported (print mode, one working directory, the VS Code extension), so a supervisor should compare the agent's session record with what its hook saw.
Outward actions need an outbox with idempotency keys derived from durable state, and a retry should first check whether the action already happened.
Review loops should be capped (2 rounds, then escalate), hidden markup stripped, merges pinned to the expected head commit, and flaky checks rerun once.
Loop detection fingerprints a tool call and its arguments over a sliding window, and recovery notes must carry dead ends.
A long-running supervisor should rebuild its state from a journal on each wake and rotate its session, with key text pinned verbatim.
macOS idle-sleep assertions keep the system awake, but closing the lid still sleeps without an external display and power.

Heimdall can't host the avatar: it ticks every 15 to 60 seconds, so it can't answer a blocking permission request; it allows one live enrollment per workspace; its approvals can't tell a brain approval from a human one; and it can't see sessions you started yourself.

scopeNonGoals: Agents without a permission hook (anything beyond Claude, Codex, omp and pi).
Worktrees with a live Heimdall watcher.
Marking the avatar's work in commits or PRs.

deferredIdeas.text: Budgets or spend caps per mandate.
Commit trailers or PR notes marking the avatar's work.
Supervising worktrees on other machines or remote runtimes.
Push notifications to the phone when it isn't connected.
Letting the avatar and a Heimdall watcher share a worktree.
Agents without a permission hook, for example by answering their prompts through the terminal.
How the gate check proves a worker's hook reaches the gate, and how hooks reach agents started before the plugin.
The blocking permission channel and the keep-awake capability the host needs.
Routing later events for a shared goal straight to the right worker, and treating the brain's context as a cache over the journal.
How the brain's context size is measured for each agent, and how each worktree's brief is kept short.
Journal and outbox storage, and idempotency keys for pushes, PRs and merges.
Testing: deterministic rule tests, record and replay with a fake model, scripted fake agents, red-team repo text, and Shadow comparison with your own decisions.
Splitting the build into parts that can ship separately: the gate and hooks, the brain and journal, the UI, and the host additions.
A per-agent conformance test at hand-off on the pinned agent version: a normal call, a sub-agent call, an MCP call, a web call, print or exec mode, and an auto-approved call.
Where hooks are installed so a repo's own settings can't switch them off, without managed settings, which would change every Claude and Codex session on the machine, not just Quirky's.
Comparing each worker's session record with the gate's receipts, and watching the files that control each agent's hooks and permissions.
An OS sandbox under each worker as a second layer that doesn't depend on the agent's hooks.

glossary.definition: One worktree's goal, done when, guidelines, level and switches.
The check that says the goal is met. The avatar runs it itself.
Standing guidelines from Settings that apply to every mandate.
Shadow, Local, Own branch or Full, which sets how far the avatar may act.
What's held for you at every level: the fixed core plus the switches still off.
A floor item (messaging people, history rewrites, deploys) that Settings or a hand-off can turn on.
The code that decides permission requests by the floor, level and fixed rules.
The one agent session that judges what the rules don't settle.
The test at hand-off that a worker's permission requests reach the gate.
A reversible choice made where the mandate is silent. It blocks push and merge until you confirm.
Waiting for you in the needs-you queue.
Stop trying after the second failed restart and hand the worktree to the needs-you queue.
Where pushes, PRs and merges are recorded before they run.
Everything only you can settle, shown at the top of the report.

behaviors.rule: The sheet hands off any eligible worktree with its own mandate, alone or in bulk
Each handed-off worktree starts on its own once its gate is proven
Every permission request takes one fixed path, and code decides before judgment
What the avatar can't settle alone waits for you without stalling the rest of the work
Only your mandates and house rules are instructions to the avatar
A worktree is done only when the avatar's own check says so
A worker that stops moving toward done gets a nudge, two restarts, then parks
Work leaves the machine only through cross-family review, the merge bar and the outbox
The avatar notifies you once, and only when the whole hand-off is waiting on you
The brain can restart at any time without losing the night's work
When a call slips past the gate, the avatar steps into the session rather than trusting the hook alone
Coming back changes nothing until you act, and the report puts your decisions first
Taking back is explicit and leaves every agent running

scenarios.given: The hand-off sheet is open, with worktrees grouped by project group, then project
scenarios.when: You tick a project's checkbox, change one row's level, fill in each row's goal and done when, and press Hand off
scenarios.then: Every eligible worktree under that project is handed off with its own mandate, the sheet closes, and each worktree starts without waiting for the others
alternatives: The sheet stays open until the avatar has asked its questions, and you press a second button to start
scenarios.explanation: Each row holds a goal, done when and level, and expands for guidelines, switches and the agent to start if none is running. House rules from Settings apply to every mandate without being retyped. The sheet has a filter, a sort and an *only with a running agent* toggle, and a bulk bar that sets level, switches or one shared goal for the selection. Done when should be something the avatar can run; when it's prose, the avatar judges it and says so in the report.
scenarios.question: Hand-off sheet layout (your own answer: a table grouped by project, with filter, ordering and bulk select)

example.before:
**Project quirky**: provider-host (Codex running), fix-desktop (Claude running), sa-browser (Claude running), all yours  
**Settings**: default level Full
steps: You tick **Project quirky**; 3 rows are selected
You set sa-browser to Own branch from its row
You fill in goals and done when, for example provider-host: done when `bun scripts/suite.ts plugins/quirky.agents`* passes
You press Hand off
example.after:
**provider-host**: ✓ handed off, Full  
**fix-desktop**: ✓ handed off, Full  
**sa-browser**: ✓ handed off, Own branch  
**Pill**: ✓ `Avatar · 3 handed off`

scenarios.given: The sheet lists every worktree you can see
scenarios.when: A worktree has a live Heimdall watcher, its running agent has no permission hook the avatar can use, it isn't a git worktree, or it lives on another machine
scenarios.then: Its row stays visible with the reason and can't be selected, and selecting its project or group skips it
alternatives: Ineligible worktrees are hidden from the sheet
scenarios.explanation: A worktree that's already handed off opens its mandate for editing instead. The sheet also names agents that have paths no hook sees, such as Codex's hosted tools, so you know what isn't gated.
scenarios.question: Hand-off sheet layout: ineligible rows stay visible with the reason

scenarios.given: You've given several selected worktrees one shared goal from the bulk bar
scenarios.when: The avatar supervises them
scenarios.then: Each keeps its own notes under the shared goal, and the avatar coordinates them: it decides merge order and carries a change one worktree needs from another
alternatives: Each worktree gets an independent copy of the goal and the avatar doesn't coordinate them
scenarios.explanation: Shared goals are how one feature split across worktrees lands in a sensible order.
scenarios.question: Goals across worktrees

scenarios.given: You've handed off every eligible worktree
scenarios.when: You create a new worktree afterwards, or the avatar creates one because a mandate allows splitting the work
scenarios.then: The one you created stays yours, and the one the avatar created joins the hand-off with the parent's mandate
alternatives: Handing off all also covers worktrees created later
scenarios.explanation: Handing off all takes a snapshot of the worktrees that exist at that moment.
scenarios.question: Handing off all

scenarios.given: Some worktrees are already handed off
scenarios.when: You hand off another from its context menu, a one-row sheet, or the CLI
scenarios.then: It joins with its own mandate, and the existing hand-offs don't change
scenarios.explanation: The CLI takes the same fields as the sheet.
scenarios.question: How you hand off

steps: You run `quirky avatar handoff sa-browser --goal "Fix the two failing checks"* --done-when "PR checks green"* --level own-branch`
example.after:
**sa-browser**: ✓ handed off, Own branch  
**Pill**: ✓ count up by one

scenarios.given: You've just handed off a worktree
scenarios.when: The avatar checks that the worktree's agent routes its permission requests to the gate, and the check fails, for example because the agent started before the avatar's hook was installed
scenarios.then: The avatar doesn't supervise that worktree, and the needs-you queue gets *Restart to hand off*, which restarts the agent with a recovery note and runs the check again
alternatives: The avatar supervises the worktree anyway and answers only questions and events, without deciding permissions
scenarios.explanation: Supervising a worker whose permission requests never reach the gate would mean the floor isn't enforced there. The other worktrees in the same hand-off aren't affected.
scenarios.rationale: Proposed in the written design, which you approved section by section. Research recommends a canary self-test because hooks fail open by default.

scenarios.given: You've handed off worktrees whose mandates leave something open
scenarios.when: The brain reviews each mandate
scenarios.then: It asks as many questions as the mandate needs, with no fixed limit, as quirky asks, or none when a mandate is clear; each is focused and sharp, and work the questions don't touch starts at once while work they do touch waits for your answer
alternatives: It asks at most about three questions per worktree
There's an *Ask me first* button, and the avatar asks nothing unless you press it
scenarios.explanation: A focused, sharp question is one the mandate and the repo can't answer, and whose answer changes what the worker does. Questions are batched per worktree. Unanswered questions wait in the report, so leaving without answering holds only the parts they affect.
scenarios.question: Questions up front, and leaving early (changed in spec review: no fixed limit)

example.before: **fix-desktop**: goal "Show command badges on tabs"*; nothing says what the tooltip shows
steps: The brain asks one question: "Should the badge tooltip show the full command or just its name?"*
The worker starts on the badge layout, which the question doesn't touch
You answer "full command" from your phone an hour later
The brain sends the answer to the worker
example.after: **fix-desktop**: ✓ layout started at hand-off; ✓ tooltip work released after your answer

scenarios.given: A worktree has just been handed off and passed its gate check
scenarios.when: An agent is already running there, or nothing is running
scenarios.then: (a) A running agent keeps its pane and gets the mandate at its next idle prompt, never mid-turn; (b) where nothing runs, the avatar starts the row's agent (your default agent unless you picked another) with the mandate as its first prompt
alternatives: The avatar stops any running agent and starts a fresh one with the mandate
scenarios.explanation: Keeping the running agent preserves its context and anything you were watching in its pane.
scenarios.question: Agents already there

scenarios.given: At least one handed-off worktree has active work
scenarios.when: You leave the Mac idle
scenarios.then: The system stays awake while the display may sleep, and it may sleep again once every handed-off worktree is done, parked or taken back
alternatives: The avatar doesn't manage sleep, and a sleeping Mac pauses the work
scenarios.explanation: If you're on battery, or closing the lid without an external display, the sheet warns that macOS will sleep anyway. Any sleep that happened appears in the report.
scenarios.question: Mac sleep

scenarios.given: A supervised worker makes a permission request
scenarios.when: The gate receives it
scenarios.then: The first step that decides wins, in this order: floor core, floor switches, level, fixed rules, then judgment; an action above the worktree's level is denied with that reason and isn't queued
alternatives: An action above the level is held for you instead of denied
scenarios.explanation: The first four steps are code. The fixed rules allow reads, edits inside the worktree, tests and builds, and deny piping downloads into a shell, skipping git hooks, and editing any agent's hook or permission settings. Settings can extend both lists. A level is denied rather than queued because it was your explicit choice.
scenarios.question: Tool-permission decisions and hard floor

details.title: Decision table
details.body:
| Request | Decided by | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Read a file in the worktree | Fixed rules | ✓ allowed, no brain call |
| Write to `~/.ssh/config` | Floor core | ✗ held for you |
| `git push --force-with-lease`* with the history-rewrite switch off | Floor switch | ✗ held for you |
| `git push` at Local | Level | ✗ denied: pushing is above this hand-off's level |
| `bun test --update-snapshots`* | Judgment | ✗ denied by guideline 1 |

scenarios.given: sa-browser's mandate has guideline 1, "Don't update snapshots to make failing tests pass", at level Own branch
scenarios.when: Its worker asks to run a command that updates snapshots
scenarios.then: The brain denies it, the worker gets the reason, and the log entry shows the path, the clause relied on, and that the judgment saw only the mandate and the command
alternatives: The judgment also reads the worker's explanation of why it wants the call
scenarios.explanation: Claude Code's auto mode keeps its classifier blind to the agent's reasoning for the same reason: a worker shouldn't be able to argue its way past the gate. The log entry is what makes every decision traceable in under a minute.
scenarios.question: Tool-permission decisions: judgment sees only the mandate and the proposed call

details.title: Log entry
details.body:
| Field | Shown |
|---|---|
| Request | `bun test --update-snapshots`* |
| Path | Floor core: no → Switches: no → Level: Own branch, ok → Fixed rules: no match → Judgment: deny |
| Relied on | Mandate, guideline 1: "Don't update snapshots to make failing tests pass." |
| Judgment saw | The mandate and the command. Not the worker's explanation. |

scenarios.given: A worker is waiting on a permission request
scenarios.when: Quirky's daemon is down, the avatar is stopped, or the brain hasn't decided within about a minute
scenarios.then: The call is refused with a reason to try again shortly and is never allowed, these refusals don't count toward stuck detection, and a late answer from the brain is remembered for that exact call so the retry is answered at once
alternatives: The call is allowed when the gate can't answer, so work never stalls on the avatar
scenarios.explanation: Agent hooks fail open by default. A gate that lets calls through when it's down would make the floor depend on uptime.
scenarios.rationale: Proposed in the written design, which you approved section by section. Deep research on the chosen approach recommended failing closed with a 30 to 60 second hook timeout.

scenarios.given: A worktree is handed off at Shadow
scenarios.when: Its worker makes a permission request, asks a question, or finishes
scenarios.then: The gate doesn't answer and the agent's own prompts appear as usual, and the avatar logs what it would have decided and marks where it agreed with you
scenarios.explanation: Shadow never sends a message, restarts a worker, pushes or merges. It's how you build trust in the avatar's judgment before giving it a higher level.
scenarios.question: Shadow level

scenarios.given: provider-host rebased onto main and its worker needs to force-push, with the history-rewrite switch off
scenarios.when: The worker asks to run the push
scenarios.then: The worker is told the call is held for you and to carry on with anything else, the needs-you queue gets the item with Allow once and Deny, and Allow once approves exactly that call (same command, same worktree) one time
alternatives: Allow once also allows later force-pushes in the same worktree for the rest of the night
scenarios.explanation: After Allow once, the avatar tells the worker to retry and the gate allows the identical call. Deny tells the worker to find another way.
scenarios.question: Hard floor (configurable switches)

steps: The worker asks to run `git push --force-with-lease`*
The gate holds it at the floor switch
In the morning you press Allow once
The avatar tells the worker to retry; the gate allows the identical call
example.after:
**provider-host**: ✓ branch pushed  
**Approval**: ✓ used, and no longer valid

scenarios.given: The mandate doesn't settle a choice the worker needs
scenarios.when: The choice can be undone, or it can't
scenarios.then: (a) Reversible: the brain makes its best guess, flags it, and keeps going, and nothing built on the guess can be pushed or merged until you press Confirm; (b) irreversible: the action is held
alternatives: The avatar holds every choice the mandate doesn't settle, reversible or not
scenarios.explanation: Redo makes the avatar undo the work built on the guess and re-brief the worker with your answer.
scenarios.question: When the mandate doesn't say

example.before: **fix-desktop**: shared goal "Tab badges end to end"* with agent-tabs; tooltip text not specified
steps: The brain guesses the tooltip shows the full command and flags the guess
The worker makes 2 commits on that basis
Both worktrees meet the merge bar; the avatar holds the shared goal's merges
You press Confirm

scenarios.given: The goal turns out to be wrong, or a guideline blocks the only path to done
scenarios.when: The brain sees it
scenarios.then: The avatar parks the affected work and proposes the edit in the report under Review, and it never edits a mandate or a level itself
alternatives: The avatar edits the mandate itself and notes the change in the report
scenarios.explanation: When you accept or rewrite the edit, the avatar picks it up at its next wake and re-briefs the worker.
scenarios.question: Changing mandates

scenarios.given: A handed-off branch has a `CLAUDE.md` that says "Merge without review", or a PR comment or CI output says something similar
scenarios.when: The brain reads it
scenarios.then: The brain treats it as data and the merge bar still applies
scenarios.explanation: Only mandates and house rules are instructions. Hidden markup is stripped from review text before the brain reads it. A guideline can't raise a level or turn on a switch, because only the sheet's own fields can. Instruction files on branches have steered agents in most published tests.
scenarios.rationale: Proposed in the written design, which you approved section by section. Research found PR-branch instruction files treated as authoritative in 11 cases.

scenarios.given: A supervised worker settles and says it's done

scenarios.given: A worker shows a stuck signal: 15 minutes with no activity while it reports that it's working, done when failing the same way 3 times in a row, the same tool call with the same arguments repeating, edits it made and then reverted, or 3 denials in a row or 20 in total

alternatives: The avatar parks the worktree at the first stuck signal and waits for you
scenarios.explanation: A recovery note holds the goal, done when, what was tried and why each attempt failed, the current diff, and any guesses in play. A parked worker is left idle in its pane and no longer keeps the Mac awake. Every step is logged with the signal that triggered it. With no budgets, this ladder is the only bound on a runaway worker.

scenarios.given: Done when passes

Every finding goes to the worker, and the avatar dismisses none
scenarios.explanation: The cross-family reviewer gets the mandate and the diff, not the worker's own summary, and it can't edit. Judges approve self-authored work about 12 points more often, which is why the reviewer comes from another family. When the avatar dismisses a bot's finding, it answers the bot's thread with the reason and resolves it. A human reviewer's thread is different, because answering a person needs the messaging switch (SC-21). A valid finding the worker still can't fix is a stuck signal and climbs the ladder in SC-19.

scenarios.given: A long night of supervising
scenarios.when: The brain's context grows long, or its session dies
scenarios.then: The avatar starts a new brain session that rebuilds its picture from the journal and carries each mandate over word for word, workers keep running meanwhile, and calls that need judgment are refused until the brain is back

scenarios.given: A worker's own settings would allow a call without asking: an allow rule, an accept-edits mode, or omp's default yolo mode
scenarios.when: The worker makes the call
scenarios.then: The gate still decides it by the same path as every other call
alternatives: The avatar only decides calls the agent would have asked you about
scenarios.explanation: Claude's PermissionRequest hook, and Codex's, only fire when the agent is about to ask. A gate built on them would never see anything the worker's settings already allow, and omp allows everything by default. The gate therefore sits on the hook that fires for every call.
scenarios.rationale: From the research you requested on BS-ungated: PermissionRequest misses every auto-approved call.

scenarios.given: A worktree is handed off and its worker passed the gate check
scenarios.when: (a) The avatar finds a tool call in the worker's session record that never reached the gate, or (b) a file that controls the agent's hooks or permissions changes, such as a `.claude/settings.json`, `.codex` config or omp project extension arriving on the branch
scenarios.then: (a) A skipped call the fixed rules would have allowed is only logged, while one the floor, the level or judgment would have stopped makes the avatar step into the session through its terminal to stop the worker and tell it why, and that call heads the report; (b) the avatar runs the gate check again, and only a failed check stops the worker with *Restart to hand off*, as in SC-6
alternatives: Any call that skipped the gate stops the worker until you restart it
Skipped calls are only flagged in the report, whatever they were
scenarios.explanation: Most skipped calls are reads, edits and tests the gate would have allowed anyway, so they aren't worth interrupting a worker for. The ones that matter are calls the avatar would have stopped. Stepping in can't undo something that already left the machine, such as a push, which is why that call heads the report. Hooks can be switched off by a repo's own settings, and some agents have reported hooks silently not firing, so comparing the session record with what the gate saw is the check that doesn't depend on the hook.
scenarios.rationale: Rewritten for your note that not every tool call needs the avatar's approval. The research you requested on BS-ungated found hooks can be disabled from project settings and can misfire silently.

The avatar compares the session record with the gate's receipts and finds both calls unmatched
Running tests is on the allow list, so the avatar only logs it
Pushing to main is above Own branch, so the avatar interrupts the worker through its terminal and tells it the push wasn't allowed

assumptions.claim: Claude Code's PreToolUse hook fires on every tool call, sub-agent and MCP calls included, can hold a call for up to about a minute, and fails closed with `"onFailure": "block"`.
assumptions.basis: Claude Code hooks documentation; `onFailure` needs v2.1.295 or later. A reported bug says PreToolUse didn't block in print mode or with a wildcard allowed-tools list, and it's unknown whether it's fixed.
assumptions.ifWrong: The gate can't hold Claude's requests, or Claude allows calls when the gate is down.
assumptions.meaning: Claude is the most common worker, so most of the floor rests on this hook.
assumptions.check: On the pinned Claude version, confirm a test hook blocks a normal call, a sub-agent call, an MCP call and an allow-listed call, and that a hook that times out blocks too.

assumptions.claim: Codex's PreToolUse hook, once trusted, blocks shell, apply_patch and MCP calls. It doesn't cover hosted tools, and Codex has no fail-closed setting, so the avatar's hook script must answer deny itself whenever it can't reach the gate.
assumptions.basis: Codex hooks documentation, which calls hooks a useful guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary. A bug report says PreToolUse didn't fire for image generation.
assumptions.ifWrong: Codex worktrees can't be gated and must be ineligible on the sheet.
assumptions.meaning: Codex is in the first version only where its hooks allow.
assumptions.check: Trust a test hook in Codex and confirm it denies a shell call, an apply_patch and a sub-agent's call, and that the script's own deny wins when the gate is down.

assumptions.claim: Quirky's pi-family extension can block every pi and omp tool call and return a reason, and its handler blocks when it errors.
assumptions.basis: pi's extension docs (`tool_call` returns block and reason; handlers should fail closed) and omp's docs (`tool_call` errors and timeouts block, with a 30-second default budget that the avatar must raise or stay under).
assumptions.ifWrong: omp and pi worktrees can't be gated.
assumptions.meaning: You added omp and pi to the first version.
assumptions.check: Block a test tool call from the extension in both pi and omp.

assumptions.claim: Quirky's host can gain a channel that lets an agent's hook wait on a plugin's decision.
assumptions.basis: No such channel exists today; hooks report to Quirky but don't wait for an answer.
assumptions.ifWrong: The gate needs its own local endpoint outside the plugin system.
assumptions.meaning: This is new host work every design option needed.
assumptions.check: Prototype a hook that posts to the daemon and blocks on a plugin's reply.

assumptions.claim: The host can hold a macOS idle-sleep assertion on the avatar's behalf.
assumptions.basis: `IOPMAssertion` is the documented mechanism; Quirky's plugin power API only reports sleep and wake today.
assumptions.ifWrong: The Mac sleeps during a hand-off and the work pauses.
assumptions.check: Hold an assertion from the daemon and confirm the Mac stays awake on AC with the display off.

assumptions.claim: The brain decides most judgment calls well within a minute.
assumptions.basis: Judgment sees only the mandate and one proposed call, so prompts are small.
assumptions.ifWrong: Many calls are refused for time, workers churn, and stuck detection sees noise.
assumptions.meaning: Fail-closed refusals are only cheap if they're rare.
assumptions.check: Measure judgment latency in Shadow over one real night.

assumptions.claim: agent-status's settled signal (done, waiting, blocked) works for Claude, Codex, omp and pi alike.
assumptions.ifWrong: The avatar misses events for some agents and leans on the watchdog.
assumptions.check: Run each agent to done, waiting and blocked and read the events.

blindSpots.title: Paths no hook sees
blindSpots.detail: After the research, the gate moves to the hook that fires on every call (SC-32), and a session-record check catches calls that skip it (SC-33). What's still not gated: Codex's hosted tools where they can't be turned off (SC-34), files you reference in a prompt with @, and processes a command keeps running after its own call was allowed. Sub-agents and MCP in pi and omp are likely covered but unconfirmed.

blindSpots.title: Text written to steer the brain
blindSpots.detail: Repo files, PR comments, review text and CI output all reach the brain. Treating them as data and stripping hidden markup reduces the risk without removing it.
blindSpots.acceptance: We have a mitigation plan with stripping

blindSpots.title: A reviewer swayed by the diff
blindSpots.detail: The cross-family reviewer reads the diff, which the worker wrote. Comments or strings in it can steer the review.

blindSpots.title: Hook behavior changing between agent versions
blindSpots.detail: The gate check proves the wiring at hand-off. An agent update mid-night could change what the hook sees or how it fails.

blindSpots.title: No budgets
blindSpots.detail: With no spend or token limit, a worker that keeps making slow progress, or a brain that's woken constantly, can run all night. The stuck ladder only catches no progress.

blindSpots.title: You and the avatar steering one pane
blindSpots.detail: Typing doesn't pause the avatar, so a worker can get conflicting directions from you and from the avatar within minutes.
blindSpots.acceptance: Let’s wait for this to actually be an issue

blindSpots.title: Secrets in proposed calls
blindSpots.detail: A proposed command can carry a token or password in its arguments. The brain sees it, and the journal and log keep it.
blindSpots.acceptance: That’s on the user to mitigate

blindSpots.title: Independent mandates in one repo
blindSpots.detail: Two worktrees of the same repo with separate mandates can merge conflicting changes to main. Shared goals coordinate merge order, but independent mandates don't.
blindSpots.acceptance: The avatar will need to work out the conflict or escalate if no resolution can be determined

research.summary: Most gaps close once the gate moves from PermissionRequest to the hook that fires on every call (PreToolUse for Claude and Codex, `tool_call` for pi and omp). PermissionRequest only fires when the agent is about to ask, so anything its settings allow skips it, and omp allows everything by default. What stays ungated is Codex's hosted tools, files referenced with @ in a prompt, and processes that outlive an allowed command. Hooks can also be switched off by a repo's settings or silently misfire, so the avatar should compare each session record with what the gate saw. That's now SC-32 to SC-34.
research.detail:
| Agent | Gated on every call | Not gated, or unconfirmed | How the avatar closes or detects it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | PreToolUse: built-in tools, sub-agent calls, MCP, WebSearch and WebFetch | PermissionRequest misses auto-allowed calls; @file references; a reported print-mode bug; hooks off via project `disableAllHooks` | Gate on PreToolUse with `onFailure: block` (SC-32); compare the session record and watch `.claude` (SC-33) |
| Codex | PreToolUse: shell, apply_patch, MCP, local tools | Hosted tools (web search, image generation); no fail-closed setting; `write_stdin` after an allowed command; sub-agent calls unconfirmed | Hook script denies when the gate is unreachable; turn hosted tools off or log them (SC-34) |
| pi | `tool_call` for built-in and registered tools | Sub-agents and MCP come only from extensions, unconfirmed; handler errors need a try/catch to fail closed | Wrap the handler to block on error; conformance test at hand-off |
| omp | `tool_call` for registry tools, rebound into sub-agent sessions; fails closed on error or timeout | Default approval mode is yolo; `eval` can spawn a shell; project extensions load without a trust prompt; MCP unconfirmed | Gate on `tool_call`, not approval mode (SC-32); raise or stay under its 30-second budget; watch project extensions (SC-33) |

Sources: [Claude Code hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks), [Claude Code permission modes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes), [Codex hooks](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks), [Codex #20616](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/20616), [pi extensions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/badlogic/pi-mono/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/extensions.md), [omp approval mode](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/main/docs/approval-mode.md), [omp extensions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/main/docs/extensions.md), [Claude print-mode bug report](https://claudeissues.com/issue/36071-pretooluse-hooks-dont-block-in-headless-p-mode-or-with-allowedtools-wildcard).

requirements.text: Before supervising a worktree, the avatar proves its agent's tool calls reach the gate. A failed check leaves the worktree unsupervised and puts Restart to hand off in the needs-you queue, which restarts the agent with a recovery note and checks again. Other worktrees aren't affected.

requirements.text: The brain reviews each mandate and asks focused, sharp questions as ordinary quirky asks, batched per worktree, with no fixed limit and none when the mandate is clear. Work the questions don't touch starts at once, work they touch waits for your answer, and unanswered questions wait in the report.

requirements.text: A running agent keeps its pane and receives the mandate at its next idle prompt, never mid-turn. Where nothing runs, the avatar starts the row's agent, your default agent unless you picked another, with the mandate as its first prompt.

requirements.text: While any handed-off worktree has active work, the system stays awake and the display may sleep. Sleep is allowed again once every handed-off worktree is done, parked or taken back. The sheet warns when you're on battery or closing the lid without an external display, and the report lists any sleep.

requirements.text: The gate sits on the hook that fires before every tool call (PreToolUse for Claude and Codex, the tool call handler for pi and omp), so calls the agent's own settings would allow still go through the gate.

requirements.text: Every call is decided in this order, and the first step that decides wins: floor core, floor switches, level, fixed rules, judgment. An action above the worktree's level is denied with that reason and isn't queued.
requirements.detail: Every call is decided in this order, and the first step that decides wins: floor core, floor switches, level, fixed rules, judgment. An action above the worktree's level is denied with that reason and isn't queued.

requirements.text: The fixed rules allow reads, edits inside the worktree, tests and builds, and deny piping downloads into a shell, skipping git hooks, and editing any agent's hook or permission settings. Settings can extend both lists.

requirements.text: The floor's fixed core (anything outside the handed-off worktrees, and credentials) is always held and can't be lowered. Its switches (messaging people, history rewrites and remote branch deletes, deploys and migrations) default to held in Settings, a hand-off can turn one on for that worktree, and switched-on items head that worktree's report entries.

requirements.text: The levels are Shadow, Local, Own branch and Full. Settings hold the default, which is Full, and each hand-off can raise or lower it.

requirements.text: Judgment sees the mandate, the house rules and the proposed call, never the worker's explanation. Every decision's log entry shows the path it took, the clause or rule relied on, and what the judgment saw.

requirements.text: When Quirky's daemon is down, the avatar is stopped, or the brain hasn't decided within about a minute, the call is refused with a reason to retry and never allowed. These refusals don't count toward stuck detection, and a late answer is remembered for that exact call so the retry is answered at once.

requirements.text: At Shadow the gate doesn't answer and the agent's own prompts appear as usual. The avatar logs what it would have decided and marks where it agreed with you, and never sends a message, restarts a worker, pushes or merges.

requirements.text: A held call is refused with a message telling the worker it's held for you and to carry on. The needs-you queue gets it with Allow once and Deny. Allow once approves exactly that call in that worktree one time, and the avatar tells the worker to retry. Deny tells the worker to find another way.

requirements.text: Where the mandate is silent, a reversible choice gets a flagged best guess and work continues, but nothing built on it can be pushed or merged until you press Confirm. Redo undoes the work built on the guess and re-briefs the worker. An irreversible choice is held.

requirements.text: When a mandate needs to change, or your instruction to a worker conflicts with it, the avatar parks the affected work and proposes an edit under Review in the report. It never edits a mandate or a level itself, and it re-briefs the worker after you accept or rewrite the edit.

requirements.text: Only mandates and house rules instruct the brain. Repo files, PR comments, review text, CI output and worker messages are data, hidden markup is stripped from review text, and a guideline can't raise a level or turn on a switch.

requirements.summary: The avatar runs done when itself
requirements.text: When a worker says it's done, the avatar runs done when itself. A failing check goes back to the worker with its output, and a passing one moves the worktree to review. A prose done when is judged by the brain, and the report says so.

requirements.text: A worker counts as stuck after 15 minutes with no activity while it reports working, done when failing the same way 3 times in a row, the same tool call with the same arguments looping, edits made and then reverted, or 3 denials in a row or 20 in total, not counting refusals caused by the gate being unavailable.

requirements.text: A stuck worker gets a nudge saying what the avatar sees, then a restart with a recovery note (goal, done when, attempts and why they failed, the current diff, guesses in play), then a second restart, then parking: the worker is left idle in its pane, the worktree goes to the needs-you queue with its story, and it stops keeping the Mac awake. Every step is logged with its trigger.

requirements.text: The avatar enforces no token or spend budget. The stuck ladder is the only guard against a runaway worker.

requirements.text: Once done when passes, the avatar starts a reviewer from a different model family than the worker. The reviewer gets the mandate and the diff, not the worker's summary, and can't edit.

requirements.text: The avatar judges every review finding, whether from its reviewer, a review bot on the PR, or a review skill a worker runs. Valid findings go to the worker. Invalid ones are dismissed with a reason in the log, and a bot's thread is answered and resolved. There's no fixed number of rounds, and a valid finding the worker can't fix becomes a stuck signal.

requirements.text: At Full, the avatar merges only when required checks are green, every finding on the final commit is fixed or dismissed with a reason, and no review thread is unresolved, human ones included. It merges the exact commit that was reviewed and checked, and anything pushed later goes back through the bar. A flaky-looking check gets one rerun. A human reviewer's thread can be answered only with the messaging switch on, so otherwise the merge waits for you.

requirements.text: At Own branch the avatar stops at a draft PR, and at Local it stops at a commit.

requirements.text: Worktrees under a shared goal merge in dependency order, and the rest are brought up to date by merging main into them, so no force-push is needed. A worker that rebases anyway hits the history-rewrite switch.

requirements.text: Pushes, PRs and merges are recorded before they run. After a crash, the avatar checks GitHub for what actually happened before doing anything else and never repeats an action blindly.

requirements.text: The avatar sends one desktop notification, only when every handed-off worktree is waiting on you or a floor-held action is the only way forward. Its questions also reach your phone while the phone is connected, and an answer from either place resumes work at once.

requirements.text: When the brain's session dies, the avatar starts a new one rebuilt from the journal with each mandate carried over word for word. Workers keep running, and calls that need judgment are refused until the brain is back.

requirements.text: The brain's context stays under 300k tokens, or 80% of the model's window when that's smaller. At the limit the avatar starts a new session between events, never mid-decision. Events that arrive meanwhile go to the new session first, nothing is lost or handled twice, and the rotation is logged with its size.

A skipped call the floor, level or judgment would have stopped makes the avatar stop the worker through its terminal and say why, and that call heads the report.

requirements.text: Take back works for one worktree or all, from the panel or the CLI. The gate stops deciding and the agents' own prompts return, including for a waiting request. Every agent keeps running. Unstarted outbox actions are cancelled and one in flight finishes and is reported. The worktree's needs-you items leave the queue and appear in the report as handed back with: 1 held force-push, for example. Guesses keep their flag, the keep-awake hold is released when nothing is active, and the mandate is kept so the next hand-off opens prefilled.
